What to Assess: Share of renewable/non-fossil electricity or installed capacity vs IPCC electricity-share benchmark
NDC Source/Page: Argentina Second NDC (Dec 2020, updated Nov 2021), UNFCCC registry PDF, '2030 Vision — Energy' section, ~p.20; ICTU annex §3
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC gives no quantified renewable/electricity target — only qualitative language that renewable generation 'will have increased significantly.' The binding 20%-by-2025 electricity target is in a separate instrument, Law 27.191, not in the NDC itself.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5–<2°C pathways: low-carbon sources ~93–97% of global electricity by 2050; electricity's share of final energy rises toward ~48–58% by 2050.
Reviewer Rationale: NDC contains no renewable metric to benchmark against a 2050 electricity-share figure — scope/time-horizon mismatch. If Law 27.191 is credited instead, actual 2025 renewable generation reached only ~15% vs the 20% national target, itself far below the AR6 2050 benchmark, per Climate Action Tracker/Ember (secondary).

What to Assess: Net-zero target year, gases/sectors covered vs IPCC net-zero trajectory
NDC Source/Page: Second NDC, 'Long-term strategy' subsection ~p.30 (commits to submitting an LTS by 2050); Argentina LTS/ELP2050 (submitted UNFCCC Nov 2022)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC itself only commits to *submitting* a strategy 'with a view to achieving carbon-neutral development by 2050.' The actual net-zero target (GHG neutrality by 2050, all gases/sectors) sits in the separate 2022 LTS, not the NDC text.
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6; WGIII Ch.3
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways reach net-zero CO2 in the early 2050s and require GHG cuts of 43% [34–60%] by 2030 and 84% [73–98%] by 2050 vs 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: 2050 GHG-neutrality timing (LTS) is broadly consistent with the AR6 net-zero-CO2 window, but the NDC's own 2030 milestone (349 MtCO2e) is rated 'Highly insufficient' by Climate Action Tracker (secondary) — emissions are projected to keep rising, not fall ~43% as AR6 requires. Net-zero goal exists but is not in the NDC document proper, and near-term trajectory is off-track.

What to Assess: Specific methane reduction commitment vs IPCC rapid methane reduction requirement
NDC Source/Page: Second NDC, ICTU §3.b/§5.d (methane covered only inside aggregate target, GWP-100 SAR); Global Methane Pledge membership (secondary: CCAC)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: No specific, quantified methane reduction commitment in the NDC — CH4 is folded into the single 349 MtCO2e economy-wide target with no sectoral sub-target. Argentina is a Global Methane Pledge signatory (30% cut from 2020 levels by 2030, collective/global, non-binding, not a national NDC commitment).
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6.2
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (>50%) no/limited-overshoot pathways: global methane emissions reduced 34% [21–57%] by 2030 relative to 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: No relevant quantified NDC commitment found for methane, matching the rubric's definition of Absent. GMP membership is a global pledge, not a national NDC target, and uses a different baseline year (2020 vs AR6's 2019) — not usable as a substitute commitment.

What to Assess: Quantified adaptation finance needs/commitments and conditionality
NDC Source/Page: Second NDC, Prologue/Executive Summary and §8 'Means of implementation'
NDC Evidence Excerpt: 35 adaptation measures listed, but with qualitative targets only. Single aggregate finance figure: mitigation+adaptation actions estimated at 'USD 15 billion, with international funding' — not disaggregated by adaptation vs mitigation, and no separate conditional adaptation-finance target.
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 WGII SPM C.3, C.5
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII documents a widening adaptation finance gap, noting most tracked climate finance still goes to mitigation and adaptation finance falls short of documented needs, especially for developing countries.
Reviewer Rationale: Some quantification exists (USD 15bn) and conditionality/means-of-implementation language is present, but the figure is combined mitigation+adaptation and not adaptation-specific, so it under-evidences the dimension relative to what 'Critical'/full-absence would imply.

What to Assess: Loss and Damage finance needs, liability/compensation references, or related commitments
NDC Source/Page: Second NDC — confirmed absent (no dedicated section); First Biennial Transparency Report (BTR1, submitted Dec 2024), Chapter 6 'Pérdidas y daños', pp.~290–304 (outside NDC scope)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: The NDC contains no dedicated loss-and-damage treatment — no L&D finance need, no liability/compensation reference, no mention of the Warsaw International Mechanism or Santiago Network. Reviewer Rationale: No relevant NDC commitment found, matching the rubric's definition of Absent for the NDC-scoped review. Flagging that a qualitative (non-quantified) L&D treatment does exist in the 2024 BTR1 if the review scope is later broadened beyond the NDC document itself.

What to Assess: Transport electrification/modal shift/sector target vs IPCC transport mitigation pathway
NDC Source/Page: Second NDC, '2030 Vision — Transport' section, ~p.20
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Commits qualitatively to intermodality, active mobility via urban land-use planning, and 'sustainable energy matrices ... focusing on gasification, biofuels, electrification of mobility and use of hydrogen,' with an 'Avoid-Shift-Improve approach' by 2030 — no quantified sectoral emissions or electrification target. Natural gas is framed as a transition fuel.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways require a 59% [42–68%] reduction in transport CO2 by 2050 vs modelled 2020 levels; light-duty-vehicle electrification is the leading near-term lever.
Reviewer Rationale: A qualitative Avoid-Shift-Improve commitment exists and is directionally aligned with AR6's demand/modal-shift + electrification logic, but sets no numeric target, so it cannot be meaningfully harmonised against AR6's quantified 59%-by-2050 metric — scope/metric mismatch rather than absence.

What to Assess: Land-use commitments, sink accounting, additionality, and offsets
NDC Source/Page: Second NDC, ICTU §3 and §5, 'Market Mechanisms' subsection, National Circumstances (forestry)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: LULUCF is not separately targeted — it is folded into the single net 349 MtCO2e economy-wide target, accounted via 2006 IPCC Guidelines with GWP-100 SAR values. NDC reserves Argentina's position on Article 6 market mechanisms pending negotiations and notes it does not estimate harvested-wood-products or natural-disturbance effects. No separate sink target or additionality safeguards beyond general REDD+ references.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AFOLU can provide 20–30% of global mitigation needed for 1.5/2°C pathways to 2050 (~8–14 GtCO2e/yr economic potential, 2020–2050), led by forest/ecosystem protection; poorly-planned afforestation risks conflicting with sustainability, and long-term additionality is uncertain.
Reviewer Rationale: Sinks are present but embedded in a single net headline figure with no separate accounting or robust additionality safeguards, and CAT's own analysis shows the reported total shifts materially (349 to 351 MtCO2e) once LULUCF is excluded and GWP is converted — methodological weakness relative to AR6's AFOLU framing.

What to Assess: Share of renewable/non-fossil electricity or installed capacity vs IPCC electricity-share benchmark
NDC Source/Page: Australia's 2035 NDC (submitted UNFCCC Sept 18, 2025) + Electricity and Energy Sector Plan 2025 (DCCEEW), p.i and body text
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Explicit quantified target: 'Renewable generation increases to reach 82%' of electricity by 2030, part of the package underpinning the NDC's 62–70% economy-wide 2035 target. Framed as enabling 'wide-spread electrification' of other sectors.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5–<2°C pathways: low-carbon sources ~93–97% of global electricity by 2050; electricity share of final energy rises toward ~48–58% by 2050.
Reviewer Rationale: A specific, quantified, primary-sourced 82%-by-2030 target exists and is directionally consistent with AR6's electricity-decarbonisation trajectory (though the AR6 figure is a 2050 endpoint, so exact numeric comparison is a time-horizon mismatch). Independent commentary (Energy Council of Australia) flags that electricity is 'doing most of the heavy lifting' while other sectors lag, which is a real but second-order concern for this dimension specifically.

What to Assess: Net-zero target year, gases/sectors covered vs IPCC net-zero trajectory
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (Sept 2025); Climate Change Act 2022 (Cth) — legislates net zero by 2050; Net Zero Plan 2025
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC commits to 62–70% below 2005 levels by 2035, 'covering all sectors of the economy and GHGs' (NDC Partnership summary of registered NDC), reaffirming the legislated net-zero-by-2050 target. Climate Action Tracker (secondary): even the top of the CCA's own 1.5°C-referenced pathway 'only reduces domestic emissions 29% below 2005 levels by 2030 and 49% by 2035' excluding LULUCF — well short of the 41%/57% CAT says is required.
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6; WGIII Ch.3
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways reach net-zero CO2 in the early 2050s, with GHG cuts of 43% [34–60%] by 2030 and 84% [73–98%] by 2050 vs 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: All-sector, all-gas net-zero-by-2050 target is legislated and timed consistently with the AR6 net-zero-CO2 window, but CAT rates the underlying 2030/2035 trajectory 'Insufficient,' and the pathway leans heavily on land-sector sequestration (up to ~180 MtCO2/yr by 2050) rather than gross emissions cuts — a real ambition/robustness gap short of 'Aligned.'

What to Assess: Specific methane reduction commitment vs IPCC rapid methane reduction requirement
NDC Source/Page: Global Methane Pledge signatory (Oct 2022, DCCEEW/Minister media release); Resources Sector Plan 2025 (industry.gov.au) — methane abatement in coal/gas; Safeguard Mechanism reforms
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Australia joined the Global Methane Pledge, 'committing to reduce global methane emissions across all sectors by at least 30% below 2020 levels by 2030' (non-binding, collective, not a national NDC sub-target). The Resources Sector Plan sets qualitative actions (coal-mine fugitive detection/abatement, Resources Methane Abatement Fund) with no quantified national methane target in the NDC itself.
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6.2
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (>50%) no/limited-overshoot pathways: global methane emissions reduced 34% [21–57%] by 2030 relative to 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: Despite the 30% GMP pledge, Climate Action Tracker (secondary, citing DCCEEW 2025a) reports Australia's total methane emissions (incl. LULUCF) are 'projected to fall to just 1% below 2024 levels by 2030' — a large gap between the pledge/AR6 benchmark and the actual projected trajectory, and no binding national target exists to close it.

What to Assess: Quantified adaptation finance needs/commitments and conditionality
NDC Source/Page: National Adaptation Plan (NAP, DCCEEW, released Sept 2025), Introduction; 2025–26 Budget
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NAP: 'There is already extensive action... with $3.6 billion committed to adaptation and resilience measures since 2022 and around $9 billion out to 2030.' The 2025–26 Budget adds $354 million in new adaptation funding plus $632.5 million over the medium term. Funding is domestic and largely unconditional (government-committed), though the NAP itself states 'there is an adaptation action shortfall across all systems, risks, jurisdictions, and geographies.'
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 WGII SPM C.3, C.5
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII documents a widening adaptation finance gap; most tracked climate finance still goes to mitigation, and adaptation finance falls short of documented needs.
Reviewer Rationale: Real, quantified, multi-year domestic adaptation funding streams exist (a stronger evidentiary position than Argentina's aggregated figure), but independent analysis (IGCC, secondary) notes the NAP 'lacks firm commitments... no clear timelines, and no flagship actions with funding attached,' which keeps this short of 'Aligned.'

What to Assess: Loss and Damage finance needs, liability/compensation references, or related commitments
NDC Source/Page: DFAT Pacific regional climate finance page; Pacific Resilience Facility (Australian Government commitment, referenced alongside the 2035 target)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: No domestic loss-and-damage finance need or liability/compensation claim is made for Australia itself (as a developed country, its L&D exposure is treated as an international-support question, not a domestic one). Internationally, Australia funds the Pacific Resilience Facility, which 'will provide grants for climate adaptation, disaster preparedness, nature-based solutions and projects which respond to loss and damage,' as part of AUD3.9 billion in climate finance delivered 2020–25 (AUD1.3 billion to the Pacific).
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII recognizes losses and damages as escalating, unequally distributed, and worsening with each increment of warming, with hard/soft adaptation limits already reached in some systems.
Reviewer Rationale: The system's default 'Absent' appears based on there being no domestic NDC-text L&D clause, but a real, quantified, named L&D-responsive finance commitment exists via the Pacific Resilience Facility — it is international-facing rather than a domestic need statement, which is the correct scope for a developed-country NDC, so 'Absent' undersells the evidence found.

What to Assess: Transport electrification/modal shift/sector target vs IPCC transport mitigation pathway
NDC Source/Page: Transport Sector Plan 2025 (Dept. of Infrastructure); Net Zero Plan; National Electric Vehicle Strategy / New Vehicle Efficiency Standard
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Sets 5 qualitative 'priority actions' (electrify and increase transport energy performance; switch to low-carbon liquid fuels where electrification isn't feasible; invest in enabling infrastructure; innovate; reduce embodied emissions) aiming to 'prevent transport from becoming the top emissions source by 2030' — no quantified transport-sector emissions-reduction percentage or electrification-share target found in the primary plan text.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways require a 59% [42–68%] reduction in transport CO2 by 2050 vs modelled 2020 levels; light-duty-vehicle electrification is the leading near-term lever.
Reviewer Rationale: The system's default score (0.00 → 'Aligned') looks like a placeholder for missing data rather than a genuine evaluation — the Transport Sector Plan is real and directionally matches AR6's electrification logic, but sets no numeric target, so it cannot be meaningfully benchmarked against AR6's quantified 59%-by-2050 figure.

What to Assess: Land-use commitments, sink accounting, additionality, and offsets
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC / Net Zero Plan (DCCEEW, Sept 2025), p.44 vicinity; Climate Change Authority 2035 Targets Advice; ACCU Scheme (Clean Energy Regulator)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: LULUCF is embedded in the headline target: the 43%-by-2030 figure includes LULUCF, but is only ~23% excluding it (Climate Action Tracker, secondary, citing DCCEEW projections). The Net Zero Plan explicitly relies on 'an increasingly large amount of carbon removals to 2050 through reforestation and other land sector activities' — IGCC (secondary) cites land sequestration growing from ~74 MtCO2e/yr (2025) to ~167 MtCO2e/yr (2050), with ACCUs (Australian Carbon Credit Units) and Article 6 international units both permitted as offsets under the Safeguard Mechanism.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AFOLU can provide 20–30% of global mitigation needed for 1.5/2°C pathways to 2050 (~8–14 GtCO2e/yr economic potential), led by forest/ecosystem protection; the chapter flags long-term additionality and permanence uncertainty for land-sink-heavy strategies.
Reviewer Rationale: The system's default score (1.00 → 'Absent') is inconsistent with the evidence — LULUCF is not absent, it is heavily and increasingly relied upon. Climate Action Tracker notes successive upward revisions to projected LULUCF sequestration have made 'the NDC target progressively easier to reach' without corresponding gross cuts elsewhere — a genuine integrity/additionality concern that argues for 'Critical' rather than either 'Absent' or a clean 'Aligned'/'Significant.'

What to Assess: Share of renewable/non-fossil electricity or installed capacity vs IPCC electricity-share benchmark
NDC Source/Page: Brazil's Second/2035 NDC (submitted UNFCCC Nov 2024, COP29); Ten-Year Energy Expansion Plan (EPE); Novo PAC infrastructure programme
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC states renewables (hydro, wind, solar) already comprise '89.1% of the country's electricity mix' and commits only qualitatively to 'seek to expand electricity generation with an increased share of technology and clean sources' — no fixed numeric 2035 renewable-share target. The Ten-Year Energy Expansion Plan projects renewables at ~86% of the electricity mix by 2034, 'indicating little change from current levels'; Novo PAC targets 80% of *added* capacity from renewables but allocates only ~12% of total plan investment to renewable energy.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5–<2°C pathways: low-carbon sources ~93–97% of global electricity by 2050. Climate Analytics' Brazil-specific 1.5°C-compatible benchmark (secondary, derived from AR6 methodology) is 97–98% renewables share in electricity generation.
Reviewer Rationale: Brazil starts from an unusually high renewable baseline (89.1%), but the NDC sets no numeric target to lock in progress, and near-term plans (Ten-Year Energy Plan, Novo PAC) show the share stagnating or declining as gas and nuclear generation expand — falling short of the ~97-98% 1.5°C-aligned benchmark rather than closing on it.

What to Assess: Net-zero target year, gases/sectors covered vs IPCC net-zero trajectory
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (Nov 2024); National Mitigation Strategy (ENM, 2025); revised National Climate Change Policy (PNMC)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC includes a goal to reach 'climate neutrality by 2050 (for all GHGs)' covering all sectors, with an interim 2035 emissions ceiling of 0.85–1.05 GtCO2e (59–67% below 2005). The National Mitigation Strategy separately sets a more ambitious 2040 carbon-neutrality goal, but for CO2 only. Brazil has not yet submitted a Long-Term Strategy to the UNFCCC.
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6; WGIII Ch.3
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways reach net-zero CO2 in the early 2050s, with GHG cuts of 43% [34–60%] by 2030 and 84% [73–98%] by 2050 vs 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: 2050 all-GHG neutrality target exists and is timed consistently with AR6, but Climate Action Tracker (secondary) rates the 2035 NDC 'not 1.5°C aligned,' noting the ambition gap versus a modelled domestic pathway 'has grown compared to 2030,' and that the target is heavily reliant on transforming the land sector into a net sink rather than genuine cuts across the rest of the economy.

What to Assess: Specific methane reduction commitment vs IPCC rapid methane reduction requirement
NDC Source/Page: Global Methane Pledge signatory (COP26, 2021); NDC 'national mitigation objectives' text (Nov 2024); Plano Clima agriculture & livestock sector plan (2025)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Brazil signed the Global Methane Pledge, committing to 'reducing 30% of its methane emissions by 2030' (collective, non-binding, 2020 baseline). The NDC references reducing non-CO2 GHGs including methane as a mitigation objective, but per investigative reporting (SUMAÚMA, secondary) the agriculture sector plan under Plano Clima 'does not call for a reduction in emissions from agriculture by 2035' — agriculture/livestock is ~half of Brazil's emissions excl. LULUCF, with ~75% of that as methane and N2O from livestock (SEEG data via CAT).
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6.2
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (>50%) no/limited-overshoot pathways: global methane emissions reduced 34% [21–57%] by 2030 relative to 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: A quantified pledge exists (GMP, 30% by 2030) but the sector responsible for the large majority of Brazil's methane — livestock agriculture — is explicitly exempted from any 2035 reduction requirement in the sectoral implementation plan, which is a direct, well-evidenced disconnect between the pledge and actual sectoral policy.

What to Assess: Quantified adaptation finance needs/commitments and conditionality
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (Nov 2024) — sustainable sovereign bonds; National Adaptation Strategy (ENA, public consultation late 2024); National Adaptation Plan (submitted UNFCCC Feb 2026)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC notes Brazil issued '$2bn in sustainable sovereign bonds' (Nov 2023 and June 2024) whose proceeds fund deforestation control, biodiversity conservation, replenishing the Climate Fund, renewable energy/clean transport, and anti-poverty programs — a real but not adaptation-exclusive figure. Brazil has since completed and submitted a full National Adaptation Plan to the UNFCCC (Feb 2026), following 16 sectoral/thematic adaptation plans developed under Plano Clima.
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 WGII SPM C.3, C.5
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII documents a widening adaptation finance gap; most tracked climate finance still goes to mitigation, and adaptation finance falls short of documented needs in developing countries.
Reviewer Rationale: Brazil now has one of the more complete adaptation planning architectures reviewed so far (ENA + 16 sectoral plans + formally submitted NAP), which argues against 'Critical'/near-absence; however, the only quantified finance figure found in the NDC itself is a mixed-use bond program, not a disaggregated adaptation-finance commitment, so full alignment can't be confirmed from NDC text alone.

What to Assess: Loss and Damage finance needs, liability/compensation references, or related commitments
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (Nov 2024) — no dedicated loss-and-damage section found; COP30 Belem outcomes (Nov 2025, hosted by Brazil) — Loss and Damage Fund operationalisation, Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: No specific loss-and-damage finance need, liability/compensation reference, or standalone L&D commitment was found in Brazil's own NDC text. As COP30 host, Brazil convened and helped finalize L&D architecture at the multilateral level (WIM, Santiago Network, FRLD operationalisation), but this is a convening/presidency role in the UNFCCC process rather than a national commitment within Brazil's own NDC.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII recognizes losses and damages as escalating, unequally distributed, and worsening with each increment of warming, with hard/soft adaptation limits already reached in some systems.
Reviewer Rationale: No relevant NDC-text commitment found, consistent with 'Absent.' Brazil's high-profile role hosting COP30's loss-and-damage outcomes is real and worth noting in context, but it is an institutional/process contribution, not a quantified national L&D commitment comparable to the other dimensions' evidence bar.

What to Assess: Transport electrification/modal shift/sector target vs IPCC transport mitigation pathway
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (Nov 2024), transport sectoral mitigation plan text; RenovaBio (National Biofuels Policy, Law 13,576/2017); Future Fuel Law (Law 14,993/2024)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC transport plan commits to 'replacing fossil fuels with electricity and biofuels,' with hydrogen anticipated by 2035 and sub-sector-specific instruments for aviation, rail, road, and maritime transport. RenovaBio does carry a quantified target — reducing the carbon intensity of transport fuels by approximately 12% by 2035 (via ~600 million CBIO credits) — but this is a fuel carbon-intensity metric, not an absolute transport-emissions target, and Climate Action Tracker (secondary) notes the NDC 'fails to include a fixed timeline for phasing out fossil fuels' in transport.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways require a 59% [42–68%] reduction in transport CO2 by 2050 vs modelled 2020 levels; light-duty-vehicle electrification is the leading near-term lever.
Reviewer Rationale: The system's default score (0.00 → 'Aligned') again looks like a missing-data placeholder rather than a genuine evaluation. A quantified sub-target exists (RenovaBio's ~12% carbon-intensity cut by 2035), but it measures fuel carbon intensity rather than absolute transport emissions, so it cannot be directly benchmarked against AR6's 59%-by-2050 absolute-emissions metric — a genuine scope/metric mismatch.

What to Assess: Land-use commitments, sink accounting, additionality, and offsets
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC / National Mitigation Strategy sectoral contributions (2025); Tropical Forests Forever Fund (TFFF, launched COP30 Nov 2025)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Following the 2035 NDC, Brazil's National Mitigation Strategy and Plano Clima sectoral contributions reveal the target relies on 'large reductions in the land use, land use change and forestry (LULUCF) sector, while projected emissions in other key sectors such as industry, agriculture, energy and transport remain stable or even increase' (Climate Action Tracker, secondary, characterizing the published sectoral plan data). Brazil launched the Tropical Forests Forever Fund at COP30 (raised $5.5–6.7bn of a $25bn goal), a performance-based payment mechanism rewarding standing forest, and the NDC signals intent to use Article 6 to sell part of its emission reductions internationally.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AFOLU can provide 20–30% of global mitigation needed for 1.5/2°C pathways to 2050 (~8–14 GtCO2e/yr economic potential), led by forest/ecosystem protection; the chapter flags long-term additionality and permanence uncertainty for land-sink-heavy strategies.
Reviewer Rationale: LULUCF is not just embedded but is explicitly the primary mechanism carrying Brazil's target, while CAT states this approach is 'effectively slowing down the much needed fossil fuel phase out and emissions reductions in other sectors' — a direct, well-evidenced substitution risk (using forest-sector gains to avoid decarbonising energy, industry, transport and agriculture) that argues for 'Critical' over the system's 'Significant.'

What to Assess: Share of renewable/non-fossil electricity or installed capacity vs IPCC electricity-share benchmark
NDC Source/Page: Clean Electricity Regulations (finalized Dec 2024, CEPA 1999); Powering Canada's Future / National Electricity Strategy (NRCan)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Federal regulation mandates a net-zero-emitting electricity grid starting in 2035 (limited, capped exceptions for CCS-equipped or short-life gas units). Primary source (Zero Emission Transit Fund page, NRCan) states 'Canada generates approximately 82% of its electricity from zero emission power sources' already, with six provinces above 90%. The National Electricity Strategy also targets doubling electricity supply by 2050 to support economy-wide electrification.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5–<2°C pathways: low-carbon sources ~93–97% of global electricity by 2050.
Reviewer Rationale: Canada is already close to the AR6 low-carbon-electricity share (82% today) and has a legislated target reaching effectively 100% non-emitting by 2035 — well ahead of AR6's 2050 horizon. Caveat: the target is 'net-zero-emitting' (includes CCS-equipped and limited-life gas), not strictly 'renewable,' which is a modest scope difference from the dimension's literal wording, but functionally the strongest D1 case reviewed so far.

What to Assess: Net-zero target year, gases/sectors covered vs IPCC net-zero trajectory
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (submitted UNFCCC Feb 11, 2025); Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act (2021)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC commits to 45–50% below 2005 levels by 2035, building on the existing 40–45%-by-2030 target, all sectors/gases, with net-zero by 2050 legislated under the CNZEAA. Notably, 'the submission did not increase ambition for 2030' (Climate Action Tracker, secondary).
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6; WGIII Ch.3
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways reach net-zero CO2 in the early 2050s, with GHG cuts of 43% [34–60%] by 2030 and 84% [73–98%] by 2050 vs 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: Legislated, all-sector 2050 target is timed consistently with AR6, but CAT rates Canada's overall climate action 'Highly Insufficient,' citing weakened policy ambition (including the 2025 removal of the consumer carbon price) and a 2035 target increase CAT calls only 'modest' relative to 2030 — a real implementation gap short of full alignment.

What to Assess: Specific methane reduction commitment vs IPCC rapid methane reduction requirement
NDC Source/Page: Canada's Methane Strategy (2022); 2030 Emissions Reduction Plan
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Canada's Methane Strategy 'outlines measures to further reduce domestic methane emissions by more than 35% by 2030, compared with 2020 levels' — a specific, quantified national target (not just a pledge), covering the oil & gas sector primarily. CAT (secondary) notes 'strengthened regulations to curb methane emissions in the oil and fossil gas sector and the introduction of an emissions cap for the same sector are still pending.'
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6.2
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (>50%) no/limited-overshoot pathways: global methane emissions reduced 34% [21–57%] by 2030 relative to 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: This is the strongest national (not just pledge-level) methane commitment reviewed so far — a specific >35%-by-2030 target roughly matching AR6's 34% benchmark in ambition, though on a 2020 rather than 2019 baseline. Falls short of 'Aligned' because key implementing regulations (oil & gas methane rules, sector emissions cap) remain unfinished per CAT.

What to Assess: Quantified adaptation finance needs/commitments and conditionality
NDC Source/Page: National Adaptation Strategy (NAS, 2023) and federal Adaptation Action Plan; Canada's international climate finance commitment (2021)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NAS launch included CAD 1.6 billion in new federal funding over 5 years; cumulative federal adaptation investment exceeds $6.5 billion since 2015 ($2 billion since fall 2022 for NAS implementation specifically), with disaster-relief-inclusive federal spending over $10 billion. Internationally, Canada doubled its climate finance commitment to CAD 5.3 billion (2021–2026) and joined the Champions Group on Adaptation Finance advocating a doubling of global adaptation finance.

IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII documents a widening adaptation finance gap; most tracked climate finance still goes to mitigation, and adaptation finance falls short of documented needs in developing countries.
Reviewer Rationale: Quantified, multi-year domestic and international adaptation finance figures are among the most detailed reviewed so far. However, independent civil-society analysis (Climate Proof Canada, secondary) argues actual need is 'at least $5.3 billion annually' — well above what's currently committed — which is real evidence of a funding gap rather than full alignment.

What to Assess: Loss and Damage finance needs, liability/compensation references, or related commitments

NDC Evidence Excerpt: Canada announced CAD 16 million in seed funding to the international Loss and Damage Fund at COP28 (established following the COP27 decision), described as building on Canada's efforts 'to address loss and damage in climate-vulnerable countries,' funded under its CAD 5.3bn international climate finance envelope. The National Adaptation Strategy also names 'loss and damages' explicitly as an international-geopolitics risk category.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII recognizes losses and damages as escalating, unequally distributed, and worsening with each increment of warming, with hard/soft adaptation limits already reached in some systems.
Reviewer Rationale: A specific, quantified, named contribution to the international L&D Fund is a stronger and more concrete piece of evidence than most countries reviewed (which had either no commitment or only general finance-facility language). $16 million is modest relative to global L&D need, which is why this falls short of 'Aligned.'

What to Assess: Transport electrification/modal shift/sector target vs IPCC transport mitigation pathway
NDC Source/Page: National Zero-Emission Vehicle (ZEV) sales mandate (regulation); Zero Emission Transit Fund (5,000 buses commitment); Zero-Emission Trucking Program ($75.8M)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Canada has a legally mandated national ZEV sales target (100% of new light-duty vehicle sales to be zero-emission by 2035, per the ZEV regulations referenced by CAT), plus dedicated federal funding programs for transit and freight electrification. However, secondary reporting (Climate Scorecard, Aug 2025) notes 'Canadians await a plan to replace carbon pricing and a revisit of Canada's mandate,' with 'EV sales... plummeting due to trade issues with the USA,' signalling political uncertainty around the mandate's durability under the new government.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways require a 59% [42–68%] reduction in transport CO2 by 2050 vs modelled 2020 levels; light-duty-vehicle electrification is the leading near-term lever.
Reviewer Rationale: This is a more concrete, quantified transport commitment than most peers reviewed (a real sales-share mandate, not just qualitative language), but it measures new-vehicle sales share rather than absolute transport-sector emissions, so it cannot be directly benchmarked against AR6's 59%-by-2050 absolute-emissions metric — and its near-term political durability is now in question per secondary reporting.

What to Assess: Land-use commitments, sink accounting, additionality, and offsets
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (Feb 2025); 2024/2025 National Inventory Report (NIR), Environment and Climate Change Canada
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Canada's 2035 target excludes LULUCF from the 2005 baseline but uses a 'gross-net' approach that partially counts LULUCF sink categories and potential engineered carbon dioxide removal toward achieving the target (Climate Action Tracker, secondary). Critically, 'with improved forestry data in the 2024 National Inventory Report, Canada's LULUCF shifted from a net sink to a net source of emissions across the entire historical period' — i.e., the land sector Canada had been counting on as a sink no longer functions as one in the updated accounting.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AFOLU can provide 20–30% of global mitigation needed for 1.5/2°C pathways to 2050 (~8–14 GtCO2e/yr economic potential), led by forest/ecosystem protection; the chapter flags long-term additionality and permanence uncertainty for land-sink-heavy strategies.
Reviewer Rationale: This is the most severe LULUCF integrity issue found among countries reviewed so far: Canada's target design assumed land-sector sink contributions that a subsequent official inventory revision showed do not currently exist (LULUCF flipped to a net source), directly undermining the credibility of the 'gross-net' accounting approach used to help meet the 2035 target.

What to Assess: Share of renewable/non-fossil electricity or installed capacity vs IPCC electricity-share benchmark
NDC Source/Page: China's 2035 NDC (submitted UNFCCC Nov 3, 2025, announced by Xi Jinping Sept 24, 2025)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC commits to increasing non-fossil energy to 'over 30% of total energy consumption by 2035' (up from a 25% target for 2030) and raising installed wind and solar capacity to 'over 3.6 TW by 2035 (≈ six times 2020 levels).' Per Climate Action Tracker (secondary), China 'has overachieved its 2030 NDC targets for renewable energy capacity... in 2024' and remains on track for its 25% non-fossil share under current policy.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5–<2°C pathways: low-carbon sources ~93–97% of global electricity by 2050.
Reviewer Rationale: Absolute capacity targets are large, quantified, and have a strong track record of overachievement, but the NDC metric (non-fossil share of *total energy*, not electricity) differs from AR6's electricity-share benchmark, and coal still supplied 58% of power generation in 2024 with 291 GW of new coal capacity in the pipeline (CAT, secondary) — the NDC calls for 'strict control' of fossil consumption rather than a phase-out, which caps this below 'Aligned.'

What to Assess: Net-zero target year, gases/sectors covered vs IPCC net-zero trajectory
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (Nov 2025); Xi Jinping's 2020 UNGA net-zero-by-2060 announcement
NDC Evidence Excerpt: For the first time, China's NDC sets an absolute (not intensity-based) target: reduce economy-wide net GHG emissions 7–10% below peak levels by 2035, 'striving to do better,' reaffirming net-zero by 2060. Climate Action Tracker (secondary) notes this 'represents a shift from intensity-based targets to absolute emission reductions for the first time, albeit from an unclear baseline' since China's peak year is not clearly defined.
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6; WGIII Ch.3
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways reach net-zero CO2 in the early 2050s, with GHG cuts of 43% [34–60%] by 2030 and 84% [73–98%] by 2050 vs 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: A real structural shift to an absolute target is genuine progress, but CAT rates it 'not 1.5°C compatible' and multiple outlets (Climate Home News, CFR) characterized the 7–10% figure as 'timid'/'underwhelming' for the world's largest emitter, with the 2060 net-zero date itself a decade later than AR6's net-zero-CO2 window.

What to Assess: Specific methane reduction commitment vs IPCC rapid methane reduction requirement
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (Nov 2025), non-CO2 GHG targets; China's Methane Emissions Control Action Plan (Nov 2023); 15th Five-Year Plan
NDC Evidence Excerpt: The 2035 NDC covers all GHGs for the first time (previously CO2-only) and sets quantified non-CO2 targets — cutting HFC production/consumption by 'at least 30%' by 2035 and raising livestock manure reuse to over 85% by 2035 — but sets no standalone quantitative methane target. Climate Action Tracker (secondary): 'the absence of standalone quantitative targets for methane... limits accountability,' and China's 2023 Methane Action Plan 'does not specify any quantitative emission reduction' target at all. The 15th FYP's non-CO2 control projects (covering methane, N2O, HFCs together) target just 30 MtCO2e of reduction — small relative to China's methane footprint, especially unaddressed coal-mine methane.
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6.2
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (>50%) no/limited-overshoot pathways: global methane emissions reduced 34% [21–57%] by 2030 relative to 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: Despite years of bilateral commitments (2021 US-China Joint Glasgow Declaration) and a dedicated action plan, China has never published a quantified national methane target, and CAT explicitly flags coal-mine methane — a major, well-understood source — as still lacking dedicated measures. This is a clearer 'no quantified commitment' case than Canada's (which has a real 35%-by-2030 target) or even Brazil's (GMP membership at least sets a number).

What to Assess: Quantified adaptation finance needs/commitments and conditionality
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (Nov 2025) — 'climate adaptive society' language; National Climate Change Adaptation Strategy 2035 (2022)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: The NDC states China will 'basically establish a climate adaptive society' by 2035, building on the 2022 National Climate Change Adaptation Strategy, with measures on monitoring/early warning, ecosystem and economic resilience, and urban resilience. Per Sino-German Cooperation on Climate Change (secondary), 'notably, no quantifiable targets are defined' for these adaptation measures — no domestic adaptation finance figure was found in the NDC or Strategy text.
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 WGII SPM C.3, C.5
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII documents a widening adaptation finance gap; most tracked climate finance still goes to mitigation, and adaptation finance falls short of documented needs in developing countries.
Reviewer Rationale: Unlike most other dimensions in China's 2035 NDC (which do carry real numbers), adaptation is explicitly qualitative only — multiple secondary sources converge on the same finding that no quantifiable domestic adaptation targets or finance figures exist, which matches the rubric's definition of 'Absent' for this dimension even though a named strategy exists.

What to Assess: Loss and Damage finance needs, liability/compensation references, or related commitments
NDC Source/Page: China South-South Climate Cooperation Fund (announced 2015, RMB 20bn/$3.1bn pledge); Xie Zhenhua COP27 statement (2022); WRI China climate finance study (2013–2022)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: China has formally declined to pay into the UNFCCC Loss and Damage Fund, with climate envoy Xie Zhenhua stating at COP27 that China 'is not obliged to contribute' as a developing country. However, China does provide L&D-adjacent bilateral support — e.g., 'the $90 million USD that China has provided to flood-hit Pakistan in 2022' — and a broader South-South Climate Cooperation Fund pledge (RMB 20bn/$3.1bn, 2015), though delivery has lagged: 'China has so far delivered 10% of its promised... Fund, or 2 billion yuan' as of COP27 (secondary, Dialogue Earth). A separate WRI analysis found China provided/mobilized $45 billion (2013–2022, ~$4.5bn/yr) in broader climate finance to developing countries, not L&D-specific.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII recognizes losses and damages as escalating, unequally distributed, and worsening with each increment of warming, with hard/soft adaptation limits already reached in some systems.
Reviewer Rationale: Real, named, quantified bilateral L&D-adjacent aid exists (Pakistan flood response) alongside a large but significantly underdelivered multilateral pledge (~10% of $3.1bn delivered after 7 years) — genuine evidence, but well short of 'Aligned' given the delivery gap and China's explicit refusal to formally contribute to the UNFCCC L&D Fund itself.

What to Assess: Transport electrification/modal shift/sector target vs IPCC transport mitigation pathway
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (Nov 2025), transport sectoral targets
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC commits to making 'new energy vehicles the mainstream in new vehicle sales' by 2035 (no numeric share given), shifting bulk cargo/container freight to waterways and rail, developing multimodal transport systems, and promoting cleaner energy in shipping and aviation. Asia Society (secondary) notes the NEV-mainstream goal is one of the targets that has 'largely already been achieved,' suggesting low incremental ambition. No absolute transport-emissions or numeric electrification-share target is set.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways require a 59% [42–68%] reduction in transport CO2 by 2050 vs modelled 2020 levels; light-duty-vehicle electrification is the leading near-term lever.
Reviewer Rationale: The system's default score (1.00 → 'Absent') doesn't match the evidence — real, if qualitative, transport commitments exist in the NDC (freight modal shift, NEV mainstreaming, shipping/aviation). But with no numeric target and 'largely already achieved' status per independent commentary, it cannot be meaningfully benchmarked against AR6's quantified 59%-by-2050 absolute-emissions metric.

What to Assess: Land-use commitments, sink accounting, additionality, and offsets
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (Nov 2025) — forest stock volume and land targets
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC commits to forest stock volume exceeding 24 billion cubic meters by 2035 (already at ~21 billion m3 per 2025 progress, European Parliament briefing, secondary), forest coverage above 26%, soil/water conservation to 75%, and protection of at least 3.15 million km² under ecological redlines. Critically, the headline 7–10%-below-peak emissions target is a *net* figure: Climate Action Tracker (secondary) states the target 'applies to net emissions, including the LULUCF sector, which is a net carbon sink in China, as well as other forms of carbon removal, making the target less transparent.'
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AFOLU can provide 20–30% of global mitigation needed for 1.5/2°C pathways to 2050 (~8–14 GtCO2e/yr economic potential), led by forest/ecosystem protection; the chapter flags long-term additionality and permanence uncertainty for land-sink-heavy strategies.
Reviewer Rationale: China's forest-sink targets are quantified and have a track record of being met or exceeded (a stronger evidentiary position than Australia, Brazil, or Canada's LULUCF entries), but CAT's core objection — that blending a genuine forest sink into the headline 'net' emissions target obscures how much of the 7–10% reduction is gross cuts vs. sink accounting — is a real transparency concern that keeps this below 'Aligned.'

What to Assess: Share of renewable/non-fossil electricity or installed capacity vs IPCC electricity-share benchmark
NDC Source/Page: Renewable Energy Directive III (Directive (EU) 2023/2413, in force since 2023); 2035 NDC (submitted UNFCCC Nov 2025)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: RED III sets a legally binding EU-wide target of at least 42.5% renewable energy share of gross final energy consumption by 2030 (aspiring to 45%), with sub-targets for transport, industry, heating/cooling and buildings, and a binding annual 1.6% increase in industrial renewable use. The 2035 NDC does not set an updated headline renewable-share figure of its own, relying on RED III's binding 2030 target as the operative benchmark.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5–<2°C pathways: low-carbon sources ~93–97% of global electricity by 2050.
Reviewer Rationale: This is one of the most detailed, legally binding renewable frameworks reviewed (sector sub-targets, binding annual increases), but the metric (share of *total* energy, not electricity) differs from AR6's electricity-specific benchmark, and even the aspirational 45% figure leaves substantial headroom before matching AR6's 2050 electricity-decarbonisation trajectory.

What to Assess: Net-zero target year, gases/sectors covered vs IPCC net-zero trajectory
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (submitted UNFCCC Nov 2025); European Climate Law amendment (2040 target, Council position Nov 5, 2025)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC sets an indicative 2035 range of 66.25–72.5% below 1990 (derived from linear trajectories between the 2030 target of 55% and the 2050 net-zero goal), alongside a newly agreed 2040 target of 90% below 1990 (with up to 5 percentage points from international carbon credits from 2036, making the effective domestic target 85%). Climate neutrality by 2050 remains the anchor goal (European Climate Law).
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6; WGIII Ch.3
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways reach net-zero CO2 in the early 2050s, with GHG cuts of 43% [34–60%] by 2030 and 84% [73–98%] by 2050 vs 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: Legally anchored, economy-wide pathway architecture is more developed than most peers, but Climate Action Tracker (secondary) rates it 'not 1.5°C compatible,' stating the EU would need at least 77% by 2035 and 90–95% domestic (excl. LULUCF) by 2040 — and criticises the 'linear trajectory' methodology itself as insufficiently front-loaded compared to a genuine 1.5°C pathway.

What to Assess: Specific methane reduction commitment vs IPCC rapid methane reduction requirement
NDC Source/Page: EU Methane Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2024/1787, final approval May 2024); EU Methane Strategy (2020); Global Methane Pledge (co-launched with US, COP26 2021)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: The EU adopted the first legally binding regulation specifically targeting methane emissions in the energy sector (oil, gas, coal), covering monitoring, reporting, verification, and leak detection/repair requirements. The EU also co-launched the Global Methane Pledge (30% cut vs 2020 by 2030, non-binding, collective). However, the binding regulation's scope is limited to the energy sector; no economy-wide quantified methane reduction target (covering agriculture and waste as well) was found in the NDC.
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6.2
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (>50%) no/limited-overshoot pathways: global methane emissions reduced 34% [21–57%] by 2030 relative to 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: Unlike most peers' voluntary pledges, the EU has actual binding law (not just a strategy or pledge) covering its largest methane source (energy sector). This is a stronger legal instrument than found elsewhere, but the absence of an economy-wide quantified target (agriculture is a major EU methane source not covered by this regulation) keeps it short of 'Aligned.'

What to Assess: Quantified adaptation finance needs/commitments and conditionality
NDC Source/Page: EU Adaptation Strategy (2021); European Commission international climate finance page; 2035 NDC (Nov 2025)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: The EU Adaptation Strategy quantifies the cost of inaction — current EU economic losses from climate-related extreme weather already exceed €12 billion/year, projected to reach at least €170 billion/year at 3°C warming — but primary implementation responsibility for adaptation stays with Member States, with the EU providing only 'enhanced proactive measures... to support them.' The EU and Member States together provided €28.5 billion in public climate finance plus €11.9 billion in mobilised private finance in 2022 (combined mitigation and adaptation, not adaptation-specific). Climate Action Tracker (secondary) notes the EU's 2035 NDC 'has not specified the amount of its planned international climate finance contributions.'
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 WGII SPM C.3, C.5
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII documents a widening adaptation finance gap; most tracked climate finance still goes to mitigation, and adaptation finance falls short of documented needs in developing countries.
Reviewer Rationale: Risk quantification (cost-of-inaction figures) is unusually rigorous, and overall climate finance volumes are large, but there is no adaptation-specific EU-level finance target, and CAT explicitly flags that the 2035 NDC itself omits a specified international finance contribution amount — a real, independently confirmed gap.

What to Assess: Loss and Damage finance needs, liability/compensation references, or related commitments
NDC Source/Page: COP28 outcomes (Dec 2023, European Commission/Consilium); Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (established 2022)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: The EU and its Member States led the initial capitalisation of the international Loss and Damage Fund, contributing more than €400 million — 'over two-thirds of the initial funding pledges' (European Commission, primary) — making the EU bloc the largest single contributor globally to the fund at its launch.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII recognizes losses and damages as escalating, unequally distributed, and worsening with each increment of warming, with hard/soft adaptation limits already reached in some systems.
Reviewer Rationale: This is the strongest, most concrete Loss and Damage evidence found among all countries reviewed so far — a specific, quantified, named contribution making up the clear majority of the fund's initial capitalisation. Held short of 'Aligned' only because €400 million remains modest relative to global L&D needs (estimated in the hundreds of billions annually).

What to Assess: Transport electrification/modal shift/sector target vs IPCC transport mitigation pathway
NDC Source/Page: EU CO2 emission performance standards for cars and vans (Regulation, revised April 2023 under Fit for 55); proposed Dec 2025 Commission amendment
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Legally binding fleet-wide targets require new cars and vans to cut CO2 emissions 55%/50% respectively by 2030 (vs 2021), reaching 100% (zero-emission) from 2035 — effectively banning sales of new CO2-emitting cars and vans EU-wide. However, a December 2025 Commission proposal would weaken this, 'allow[ing] a range of vehicle technologies to remain in play, including hybrids, plug-in hybrids, and range extenders... in addition to full EVs and hydrogen vehicles' (ESG Today, secondary), rolling back the 100% zero-emission requirement currently under review by Parliament and Council.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways require a 59% [42–68%] reduction in transport CO2 by 2050 vs modelled 2020 levels; light-duty-vehicle electrification is the leading near-term lever.
Reviewer Rationale: This is the most stringent, legally binding new-vehicle target reviewed among all countries so far (100% zero-emission new sales by 2035, not just a share/mandate), which is directionally very strong even though its metric (new-vehicle sales) differs from AR6's absolute-transport-emissions benchmark. Critically, this target is actively being weakened as of December 2025 — a live rollback risk that should be watched in any update.

What to Assess: Land-use commitments, sink accounting, additionality, and offsets
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (Nov 2025); EU LULUCF Regulation (2030 sink target)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: The EU maintains a separate, quantified LULUCF target of a 310 MtCO2 net sink by 2030, of which only 225 MtCO2 can be counted toward the overall 55% 2030 target (a partial-crediting cap, more rigorous than fully counting all sink gains). However, Climate Action Tracker (secondary) states the EU 'has not provided any LULUCF targets for 2035, nor 2040' — the exact horizon years covered by the current NDC and 2040 target.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AFOLU can provide 20–30% of global mitigation needed for 1.5/2°C pathways to 2050 (~8–14 GtCO2e/yr economic potential), led by forest/ecosystem protection; the chapter flags long-term additionality and permanence uncertainty for land-sink-heavy strategies.
Reviewer Rationale: The 2030 accounting design (a hard cap on how much of the sink can count toward the target) is more rigorous than most peers' 'net' approaches, but the complete absence of any LULUCF target for 2035 or 2040 — right when the EU's headline 66.25–72.5% and 90% targets apply — is a real, independently flagged transparency gap that prevents a fuller alignment rating.

What to Assess: Share of renewable/non-fossil electricity or installed capacity vs IPCC electricity-share benchmark
NDC Source/Page: India's NDC (2031-2035), submitted UNFCCC April 24, 2026, Union Cabinet approval March 25, 2026
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC commits to 60% of installed electric power capacity from non-fossil sources by 2035 (up from a 50% target for 2030, which India already reached five years early — 52.57% as of Feb 2026). India also met its first NDC's 40% target nine years ahead of schedule. However, per Climate Action Tracker (secondary), 'non-fossil fuel sources now account for more than 50% of India's installed power capacity, [but] they contribute to less than 30% of actual electricity generated' — coal still supplies 70–75% of actual generation due to intermittency and grid/storage constraints.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5–<2°C pathways: low-carbon sources ~93–97% of global electricity by 2050.
Reviewer Rationale: India has the strongest track record of any country reviewed for hitting (and beating) its own renewable capacity targets early, but the capacity-vs-generation gap is a genuine structural caveat — installed non-fossil capacity is not yet translating into a comparable share of actual electricity generated, and CAT separately rates the prior 50%-by-2030 target 'Highly insufficient' against a 1.5°C-modelled pathway.

What to Assess: Net-zero target year, gases/sectors covered vs IPCC net-zero trajectory
NDC Source/Page: India's NDC (2031-2035), April 2026; net-zero-by-2070 announcement (COP26, 2021)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC sets an emissions-*intensity* target (GHG per unit of GDP) of 47% below 2005 levels by 2035, up from 45% by 2030 (already at 36% as of 2020), covering all sectors and gases. Net-zero remains targeted for 2070. Per Carbon Brief (secondary), 'by setting an intensity target, India would be able to continue increasing its emissions as its economy grows' — there is no absolute, economy-wide GHG target. Climate Action Tracker (secondary) states the 2022 NDC 'will not drive real world emission reductions beyond its current level of climate action' and explicitly recommends India 'adopt a national, economy-wide GHG emissions target.'
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6; WGIII Ch.3
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways reach net-zero CO2 in the early 2050s, with GHG cuts of 43% [34–60%] by 2030 and 84% [73–98%] by 2050 vs 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: This assessment strictly compares India's pathway design to the global AR6 benchmark, as the workbook rubric specifies — it does not apply an equity/fair-share adjustment for India's developing-country status and low per-capita emissions, which India itself invokes (CBDR-RC) as the basis for its 2070 date and intensity-based design. On the literal benchmark comparison, CAT's own assessment that the target structurally 'will not drive real world emission reductions' as the economy grows is a strong, direct signal of gap severity independent of the equity debate.

What to Assess: Specific methane reduction commitment vs IPCC rapid methane reduction requirement
NDC Source/Page: India's NDC (2031-2035), April 2026; Global Methane Pledge (non-signatory status)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: India's NDC contains no standalone quantified methane target; methane is only implicitly covered within the aggregate emissions-intensity metric (per Carbon Brief, the intensity target 'covers all gases... such as methane and nitrous oxide'). Climate Action Tracker (secondary, 2023) states plainly: 'India is amongst one of the few top methane emitters, along with China and Russia, that has not signed the Global Methane Pledge.' Ember (secondary) separately notes coal-mine methane abatement remains a largely untapped 'low-hanging opportunity' with no dedicated policy found.
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6.2
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (>50%) no/limited-overshoot pathways: global methane emissions reduced 34% [21–57%] by 2030 relative to 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: Unlike every other country reviewed so far, India has neither a national quantified methane target nor even a voluntary pledge-level commitment (GMP membership) — this is the clearest 'no relevant commitment found' case among the countries reviewed, matching the rubric's definition of Absent.

What to Assess: Quantified adaptation finance needs/commitments and conditionality
NDC Source/Page: India's NDC (2031-2035), April 2026; Green Climate Fund / GEF / Adaptation Fund disbursements to India (secondary, Greenpeace India)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Carbon Brief (secondary) states plainly: 'the 1,200-word press release announcing the approval of India's new NDC for 2035 is thin on detail. For example, it did not spell out any climate-finance needs for adaptation, mitigation or climate change-induced loss and damage.' The NDC text itself states commitments 'are contingent upon the receipt of due support, including its due share of international climate finance.' As a recipient (not provider), India has received cumulative international support including USD 803.9 million from the Green Climate Fund, USD 346.52 million from the GEF, and USD 16.86 million from the Adaptation Fund — described by Greenpeace India (secondary) as 'modest compared to the challenges at hand.'
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 WGII SPM C.3, C.5
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII documents a widening adaptation finance gap; most tracked climate finance still goes to mitigation, and adaptation finance falls short of documented needs in developing countries.
Reviewer Rationale: Multiple independent sources converge on the same finding: India's NDC explicitly does not quantify adaptation finance needs or commitments, unlike most dimensions in the same NDC (which do carry real numbers). This matches the rubric's definition of Absent even though India does receive (modest) international adaptation finance through existing multilateral funds outside the NDC text itself.

What to Assess: Loss and Damage finance needs, liability/compensation references, or related commitments
NDC Source/Page: India's NDC (2031-2035), April 2026
NDC Evidence Excerpt: As with adaptation finance, Carbon Brief (secondary) confirms India's NDC 'did not spell out any climate-finance needs for... climate change-induced loss and damage' — despite India's own high vulnerability (a cited 55% rise in heat-related deaths 2000–2020 and over 80% of districts facing extreme climate risk, per secondary sources). No L&D finance need, liability reference, or related commitment was found in the NDC text.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII recognizes losses and damages as escalating, unequally distributed, and worsening with each increment of warming, with hard/soft adaptation limits already reached in some systems.
Reviewer Rationale: No relevant NDC commitment found — directly confirmed by independent analysis, matching the rubric's definition of Absent. Notably, this is a case where a highly climate-vulnerable country's own NDC omits any L&D framing at all, in contrast to several developed-country NDCs reviewed that at least reference international L&D contributions or facilities.

What to Assess: Transport electrification/modal shift/sector target vs IPCC transport mitigation pathway
NDC Source/Page: PM E-DRIVE scheme (successor to FAME I/II, launched 2024); COP26 100% EVs declaration (signed by India, 2021)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: India signed the COP26 100% EVs declaration with a focus on two- and three-wheelers, and separately has floated a plan for all two-wheelers to be electric by 2026. PM E-DRIVE provides INR 36.79 billion (USD 438 million) in incentives for battery-powered two/three-wheelers, ambulances, trucks and other EVs, following FAME I/II's INR 100bn+115bn outlay. However, Climate Action Tracker (secondary) notes 'overall adoption of EV is slow,' and separately flags that 'plans to shift long-haul trucks to LNG risk locking in fossil fuel use.' No absolute transport-sector emissions target or economy-wide electrification-share target was found in the NDC itself.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways require a 59% [42–68%] reduction in transport CO2 by 2050 vs modelled 2020 levels; light-duty-vehicle electrification is the leading near-term lever.
Reviewer Rationale: The system's default score (1.00 → 'Absent') undersells real, quantified financial incentive programs and an ambitious (if informal) two-wheeler EV target. But none of this is expressed as an absolute transport-emissions or economy-wide electrification-share figure comparable to AR6's 59%-by-2050 metric, and the concurrent LNG-truck lock-in risk cuts against the incentive schemes' net direction.

What to Assess: Land-use commitments, sink accounting, additionality, and offsets
NDC Source/Page: India's NDC (2031-2035), April 2026
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC commits to an additional carbon sink of 3.5–4.0 billion tonnes CO2e through enhanced forest and tree cover by 2035, up from the prior 2.5–3.0 billion tonne target for 2030. As of 2025, India reports having already created 2.29 billion tonnes CO2e of additional sink since 2005, putting the 2030 milestone within close reach. Notably, per Climate Action Tracker (secondary, 2023), 'India did not sign up to the COP26 forest declaration' on halting and reversing forest loss by 2030, a separate international commitment.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AFOLU can provide 20–30% of global mitigation needed for 1.5/2°C pathways to 2050 (~8–14 GtCO2e/yr economic potential), led by forest/ecosystem protection; the chapter flags long-term additionality and permanence uncertainty for land-sink-heavy strategies.
Reviewer Rationale: This is a well-quantified, separately tracked (not blended into a 'net' headline figure) sink target with credible progress data, a stronger transparency position than most peers reviewed. It falls short of 'Aligned' mainly because it is not benchmarked against AR6's AFOLU mitigation-share methodology, and continued coal expansion elsewhere in India's energy system means the sink target is not paired with a corresponding absolute-emissions constraint.

What to Assess: Share of renewable/non-fossil electricity or installed capacity vs IPCC electricity-share benchmark
NDC Source/Page: Indonesia's Second NDC (SNDC, submitted UNFCCC Oct 27, 2025), referencing the National Energy Policy; Just Energy Transition Partnership (JETP, 2022, separate from NDC)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC references the National Energy Policy's primary energy supply mix targets: 19–23% renewable energy by 2030, 36–40% by 2040, 70–72% by 2060. Separately, the JETP (an international partnership, not part of the NDC itself) targets 44% on-grid renewable power by 2030, up from 15% in 2023 — a more ambitious figure than the NDC's own energy-mix target, but JETP financing 'remains dominated by loans' (Climate Action Tracker, secondary) and implementation lags.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5–<2°C pathways: low-carbon sources ~93–97% of global electricity by 2050. CAT's Indonesia-specific 1.5°C-compatible benchmark (secondary) is 55–82% renewable power by 2030.
Reviewer Rationale: The NDC's own headline renewable target (19–23% of the total energy mix by 2030) is dramatically below even the separate JETP power-sector goal (44% by 2030), which itself falls well short of the 55–82% CAT says is needed for 1.5°C alignment — a large, multi-layered gap between the NDC text, the country's own more ambitious side-agreement, and the science-based benchmark.

What to Assess: Net-zero target year, gases/sectors covered vs IPCC net-zero trajectory
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (Oct 2025); Long-Term Strategy for Low Carbon and Climate Resilience (LTS-LCCR, submitted 2021)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Indonesia targets net zero by 2060 'or sooner.' However, the unconditional 2035 scenario shows emissions rising 56% above 2019 levels by 2035, continuing to rise for 25 years and peaking in 2050 'at more than double 2019 levels' (excl. LULUCF) (Climate Action Tracker, secondary). The conditional (internationally-supported) scenarios offer only marginally stronger near-term reductions and still rely on steep post-2035 cuts to reach net zero.
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6; WGIII Ch.3
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways reach net-zero CO2 in the early 2050s, with GHG cuts of 43% [34–60%] by 2030 and 84% [73–98%] by 2050 vs 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: While CAT itself calls the 2060 net-zero *date* 'ambitious and broadly aligned' for a developing economy, the near-term pathway text of the NDC directly undermines that framing: an unconditional scenario with emissions still rising 25 years from now, peaking at double 2019 levels in 2050, is fundamentally inconsistent with any AR6-aligned trajectory regardless of the eventual net-zero year.

What to Assess: Specific methane reduction commitment vs IPCC rapid methane reduction requirement
NDC Source/Page: 2035 NDC (Oct 2025); University of Maryland/CGS working paper on Indonesia's 2035 NDC and net-zero pathways (2025)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: No quantified methane target was found in the NDC. Independent academic analysis (CGS, secondary) states plainly: 'Policy attention to methane (CH4) and other non-CO2 gases is largely missing, with high data uncertainty.' Climate Action Tracker (secondary) confirms: 'Major sources, including agricultural methane, landfill gas, and coalmine methane, remain largely unaddressed, despite being recognised as low-cost, high-impact mitigation opportunities.'
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6.2
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (>50%) no/limited-overshoot pathways: global methane emissions reduced 34% [21–57%] by 2030 relative to 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: Two independent sources converge on the same finding — no methane-specific policy attention or quantified target exists in Indonesia's NDC, despite methane being explicitly flagged as a 'low-cost, high-impact' opportunity being left on the table. This matches the rubric's definition of Absent.

What to Assess: Quantified adaptation finance needs/commitments and conditionality
NDC Source/Page: Second NDC (Oct 2025); National Adaptation Plan (NAP) 2026–2030, submitted UNFCCC 2025
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC states USD 18.5 billion (IDR 304.8 trillion) was allocated for climate-related purposes 2020–2023, and estimates a total investment need of USD 472.6 billion for 2030–2035 across energy, agriculture, FOLU and waste sectors. Neither figure is disaggregated between mitigation and adaptation, or between domestic and international sources — Climate Action Tracker (secondary) explicitly notes the $472.6bn figure is presented 'without distinguishing between domestic investment and international climate finance needs.' A full National Adaptation Plan (2026–2030, pathway toward 2035) was separately submitted to the UNFCCC in 2025.
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 WGII SPM C.3, C.5
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII documents a widening adaptation finance gap; most tracked climate finance still goes to mitigation, and adaptation finance falls short of documented needs in developing countries.
Reviewer Rationale: A formal NAP and large aggregate finance figures are genuine evidence of adaptation planning and cost awareness, but the consistent lack of adaptation-specific disaggregation (flagged independently by CAT) means the true scale of adaptation-dedicated finance cannot be confirmed from the NDC text.

What to Assess: Loss and Damage finance needs, liability/compensation references, or related commitments
NDC Source/Page: Second NDC (Oct 2025), adaptation section
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Per WRI Indonesia (secondary summarizing NDC content), 'the government assesses research needs and gaps related to loss and damage, including slow-onset events and extreme disasters' — a real but preliminary, research/assessment-stage reference rather than a quantified finance need or funded program. Separately, academic analysis (Apresian, 2025) documents that Indonesian government agencies (BAPPENAS and the Ministry of Environment and Forestry) currently use different methods to measure loss and damage, producing inconsistent figures between planning documents.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AR6 WGII recognizes losses and damages as escalating, unequally distributed, and worsening with each increment of warming, with hard/soft adaptation limits already reached in some systems.
Reviewer Rationale: The system's default score (0.00 → 'Aligned') is a poor fit — Indonesia has real but nascent L&D content in its NDC (a commitment to *assess* needs and gaps, not a funded program or harmonised methodology), and independent research shows measurement of loss and damage is currently inconsistent even within the Indonesian government itself.

What to Assess: Transport electrification/modal shift/sector target vs IPCC transport mitigation pathway
NDC Source/Page: Presidential Decree No. 55/2019; National Industry Masterplan (RIPIN) 2015-2035; Second NDC (Oct 2025) mitigation priorities
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Indonesia's SNDC lists 'accelerating electric vehicle and biofuel deployment' among its mitigation priorities. The quantified EV targets live in adjacent instruments: 15 million EVs by 2030 (1.97 million electric cars, 12.9 million electric motorcycles), and separate production targets of 6 million two/three-wheeler EVs by 2025 and 12 million by 2035 (RIPIN). Academic analysis (ADB, secondary, referencing the prior NDC cycle) notes transport mitigation historically relied mainly on 'biofuel and natural gas to substitute petroleum' rather than a structural transport-emissions target.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways require a 59% [42–68%] reduction in transport CO2 by 2050 vs modelled 2020 levels; light-duty-vehicle electrification is the leading near-term lever.
Reviewer Rationale: The system's default score (0.00 → 'Aligned') again looks like a placeholder — real, quantified EV adoption and production targets exist, and the newest NDC references EV acceleration directly, but none of this is expressed as an absolute transport-sector emissions target comparable to AR6's 59%-by-2050 benchmark.

What to Assess: Land-use commitments, sink accounting, additionality, and offsets
NDC Source/Page: Second NDC (Oct 2025); FOLU Net Sink 2030 program (launched COP26, 2021)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: The FOLU Net Sink 2030 target pledges net negative Forestry and Other Land Use emissions of 140 MtCO2e by 2030 and 340 MtCO2e by 2050. The SNDC increases the sector's expected role further, with FOLU projected to absorb 118 MtCO2e in 2030 and 206 MtCO2e in 2035 — described by an Indonesian government official as the 'sector of hope, contributing the largest emission reductions' (Mongabay, secondary). Climate Action Tracker (secondary) states the '2035 NDC remains heavily reliant on LULUCF sinks to offset the continued growth of fossil fuel emissions,' with the FOLU target's credibility 'now being questioned amid calls for a “more realistic” approach' and ongoing food-estate-driven deforestation continuing in forest and peat areas.
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: AFOLU can provide 20–30% of global mitigation needed for 1.5/2°C pathways to 2050 (~8–14 GtCO2e/yr economic potential), led by forest/ecosystem protection; the chapter flags long-term additionality and permanence uncertainty for land-sink-heavy strategies.
Reviewer Rationale: This is among the most extreme LULUCF-reliance cases reviewed: rather than merely supplementing gross cuts elsewhere, the forest sink is explicitly positioned as the primary mitigation mechanism while fossil energy emissions are allowed to keep rising, and independent academic modelling separately finds the conditional target 'requires a net-zero land sink before 2030... but allows energy emissions to increase by 65%' — a direct substitution of land-sink accounting for real energy-sector decarbonisation.

What to Assess: Share of renewable/non-fossil electricity or installed capacity vs IPCC electricity-share benchmark
NDC Source/Page: Japan's Second NDC (submitted UNFCCC Feb 18, 2025); 7th Strategic Energy Plan / GX Basic Policy (revised 2025)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Japan's revised energy strategy targets renewables at 40–50% of the electricity mix by FY2040, with nuclear contributing another ~20% (non-fossil ~60–70% by 2040). Climate Action Tracker (secondary) recommends Japan 'set new electricity mix targets for 2035 in the new Basic Energy Plan in line with the upcoming NDC target year' — implying no explicit 2035 electricity-mix figure was set alongside the 2035 NDC itself. The GX Basic Policy 'does not provide concrete emissions reduction targets; instead, it promotes the development of so-called “clean coal” technologies... inconsistent with pathways required to limit global warming to below 1.5°C' (CAT, secondary).
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5–<2°C pathways: low-carbon sources ~93–97% of global electricity by 2050.
Reviewer Rationale: A real, quantified 2040 non-fossil target exists (and is fairly strong at 60–70%), but there is a notable gap for 2035 specifically — the exact year the current NDC covers — and continued promotion of 'clean coal' technology is independently flagged as inconsistent with the pathway needed.

What to Assess: Net-zero target year, gases/sectors covered vs IPCC net-zero trajectory
NDC Source/Page: Japan's Second NDC (Feb 2025)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: NDC sets a 60% reduction by FY2035 and 73% by FY2040 (vs FY2013), explicitly designed as 'points on a straight-line trajectory' (linear pathway) between the 2030 target (46%) and net-zero by 2050. This design was adopted despite 'more than 80% of the 3,000-plus comments the government received calling for higher targets' (Climate Home News, secondary). We Mean Business Coalition/Japan Climate Initiative (secondary) state the targets 'are less ambitious than the global average reductions required to keep the 1.5°C goal within reach, and are insufficient given Japan's developed country status.'
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6; WGIII Ch.3
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (no/limited overshoot) pathways reach net-zero CO2 in the early 2050s, with GHG cuts of 43% [34–60%] by 2030 and 84% [73–98%] by 2050 vs 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: A linear (rather than front-loaded) trajectory to net-zero directly conflicts with AR6's finding that early, steep cuts matter more than a straight-line path to the same endpoint — and multiple independent analyses, plus Japan's own public consultation majority, judged the resulting targets insufficient for a developed economy's fair share of 1.5°C-aligned effort.

What to Assess: Specific methane reduction commitment vs IPCC rapid methane reduction requirement
NDC Source/Page: Japan's Second NDC (Feb 2025); Global Methane Pledge Champion statements (Japan, 2024)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Japan's NDC sets a quantified target: 'methane emissions reduction by 11% from the level of FY2013,' bringing methane down to an estimated 26.7 million t-CO2eq by FY2030 (GMP Methane Action Update, Sept 2024). Japan is also a Global Methane Pledge 'Champion' alongside the US, EU, Canada and Germany, publicly calling on 'every Party to include absolute target of methane' in their NDCs — a notably more ambitious international ask than Japan's own 11% domestic figure.
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report SPM B.6.2
IPCC Evidence Excerpt: 1.5°C (>50%) no/limited-overshoot pathways: global methane emissions reduced 34% [21–57%] by 2030 relative to 2019.
Reviewer Rationale: Japan is one of relatively few countries reviewed with an actual quantified national methane target (not just GMP membership), which is genuine evidence — but the 11% figure is well below both the ~34% AR6 benchmark and the 30% collective GMP goal Japan itself champions internationally, a real ambition gap between Japan's international advocacy and its own domestic target.

What to Assess: Quantified adaptation finance needs/commitments and conditionality
NDC Source/Page: Japan's Climate Change Adaptation Plan (Cabinet-approved Oct 22, 2021); COP29 finance pledge (Nov 2024, Ministry of the Environment)
NDC Evidence Excerpt: Domestically, Japan's Adaptation Plan sets sector-specific KPIs for adaptation measures. Internationally, Japan pledged USD 70 billion in public and private climate support for developing countries through 2025 at COP29, explicitly 'doubling adaptation funding' (amount for adaptation specifically not itemised), and has contributed up to USD 3 billion cumulatively to the Green Climate Fund (second-largest contributor after the UK). However, Climate Transparency (secondary) finds 'most of the country's climate finance remains dedicated to mitigation, failing to achieve a balance with adaptation,' and that 'Japan mostly provides its finance as loans rather than grants.'
IPCC Source/Page: IPCC AR6 WGII SPM C.3, C.5
